ideas.title: Graph-Laplacian residual for network SIR PINNs
ideas.statement: Adding the residual of a network SIR model with Laplacian coupling, $\dot I_i = \beta_i S_i I_i / N_i - \gamma I_i - \kappa \sum_j L_{ij} I_j$, to the PINN loss lets a single model recover node-wise transmission rates $\beta_i$ from incidence observed at only a subset of nodes.
ideas.rationale: The Laplacian term propagates information from observed to unobserved nodes, so the physics loss acts as a spatial regulariser in the same way the ODE residual regularises the time series in the single-population PINN.
ideas.novelty_check: New relative to the parents: neither note handles unobserved nodes. Network-coupled PINNs probably exist for diffusion PDEs on graphs; a literature search on 'physics-informed graph neural network epidemic metapopulation' would show whether node-wise $\beta_i$ recovery under partial observation has been studied.
ideas.test: Synthetic 50-node Erdős–Rényi network, observe 30% of nodes with 10% noise; compare the error in $\beta_i$ against independent per-node PINNs and against a model without the Laplacian residual.
assumptions: The contact graph and coupling strength $\kappa$ are known
Recovery rate $\gamma$ is shared by all nodes
risks: Unobserved nodes may be unidentifiable when weakly connected
Training cost grows with the number of nodes
ideas.next_step: Write the network SIR simulator and generate the 50-node synthetic dataset.

ideas.title: Learn the mobility graph from epidemic curves
ideas.statement: Inverting the network problem — treating the coupling weights $w_{ij}$ as unknown and the rates as known — allows a PINN to infer an effective mobility network from node-level incidence curves.
ideas.rationale: The parent method already estimates unknown coefficients from trajectories; edge weights are just more coefficients, and incidence curves carry timing information about how infection moves between nodes.
ideas.novelty_check: Swapping the unknowns turns rate estimation into network inference. Network reconstruction from epidemic data is an established field, so the new element would be the physics-informed formulation; a search on 'network inference from epidemic time series' is needed before investing time.
ideas.test: Recover a known 10-node weighted graph from simulated curves; measure edge-weight error and how it degrades with noise and with the number of observed epidemic waves.
risks: Severe non-identifiability: many graphs fit the same curves
ideas.next_step: Run a quick identifiability check: perturb one edge weight and measure the change in the incidence curves.

ideas.title: Identifiability analysis before PINN training
ideas.statement: Running a structural identifiability analysis on the network SIR model before training tells which of $\beta_i$, $\rho$ and $I_i(0)$ a PINN can estimate, and which require priors or extra data such as serosurveys.
ideas.rationale: PINNs return a number for every parameter even when the data cannot determine it; an identifiability step separates genuine estimates from artefacts of initialisation and regularisation.
ideas.novelty_check: Identifiability analysis is standard in mathematical epidemiology; the contribution would be a workflow coupling it to PINN design for network models. Not new as a method, possibly useful as a methodological paper.
ideas.test: Apply differential-algebra identifiability analysis to a 3-node network SIR model with reporting fraction; check that PINN estimates of non-identifiable parameters vary across random seeds while identifiable ones do not.
assumptions: Symbolic identifiability tools scale to small networks
risks: Structural identifiability ignores noise (practical identifiability may still fail)
ideas.next_step: Write the 3-node model in SymPy and list its observable outputs.
